title: Specification Overfitting in Artificial Intelligence
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of "specification overfitting" in AI systems: cases where improving one formally specified metric (such as fairness, robustness, or a task-specific capability) leads to worse overall task performance or degradation on other important specifications. The authors argue that AI evaluation increasingly relies on proxy metrics for high-level requirements, but these metrics can be over-optimized in ways that create harmful mismatches between the measured quantity and the real-world goal.

To study this issue, the paper presents a comprehensive survey of 74 AI papers from major conferences and journals published between 2018 and mid-2023. The surveyed work spans NLP, computer vision, reinforcement learning, tabular data, and graph learning, and the authors classify each paper by the type of specification measured, the way it is measured (example-based or metric-based), whether the paper attempts to improve the specification, and whether it analyzes possible negative effects on task performance or other specifications.

The paper is not an empirical study of students or any educational intervention. It is a conceptual and taxonomic analysis of AI research and the legal/regulatory implications of specification metrics, especially in the context of AI standardization and the EU AI Act. The authors conclude that many papers implicitly guard against overfitting by reporting task performance or multiple specification metrics, but few explicitly discuss the scope, assumptions, or recommended role of specification metrics in system development. They call for clearer best practices to avoid optimizing narrow metrics at the expense of broader system quality.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual survey / taxonomy paper, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It does not use an experimental, quasi-experimental, or correlational design with K-12 learner outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct educational outcome impact; it synthesizes prior AI safety/specification literature and discusses governance implications rather than testing student-facing effects.
